strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: reducing the modality and sequence-length mismatch between speech tokens and text tokens for speech-text language modeling.

The central idea of deriving speech tokens aligned to ASR text tokens via an ASR-initialized encoder/aggregator and reconstruction objective is intuitive, practically motivated, and potentially useful.

The reconstruction results are promising: TASTE achieves competitive WER, UTMOS, speaker similarity, emotion consistency, and duration consistency at a much lower estimated bitrate than several tokenizer baselines.

The downstream evaluation suggests that text-aligned tokenization can make LoRA adaptation of a text LLM into a spoken language model more effective than a simple S3-token baseline, especially on StoryCloze and several SALMON acoustic tests.
The paper is reasonably organized and includes enough architectural detail to understand the proposed tokenizer, decoder, and two SLM variants at a high level.
weaknesses: The empirical support for the main spoken-language-modeling claims is incomplete. The SLM evaluation is limited to likelihood-based discrimination on SALMON and StoryCloze, with no direct evaluation of generated speech quality, dialogue ability, latency, robustness, or human preference, despite claims about generating reasonable and natural speech/text continuations.

The comparisons are not fully convincing. Prior systems differ substantially in model size, training data, fine-tuning regime, and modality setup; the main learned baseline with S3 tokens is weak, while stronger contemporary systems such as Moshi/mini-omni-style approaches are discussed but not experimentally compared.

Important ablations are missing: ASR initialization versus random/SSL initialization, the proposed shallow-value cross-attention versus standard cross-attention, number/codebook size of RVQ layers, word-level averaging/alignment choices, frozen versus trainable encoder, transcript quality, and token versus embedding modeling under matched settings.

The method depends on text transcripts/ASR outputs during tokenization and alignment, but the paper does not sufficiently analyze ASR errors, out-of-domain speech, multilingual settings, punctuation/tokenization mismatch, or how the approach behaves when transcripts are unavailable or noisy.

The reconstruction evaluation is somewhat hard to interpret because TASTE uses external components such as CosyVoice S3 units, speaker embeddings, and a pretrained vocoder. This makes it unclear how much of the performance comes from the proposed text-aligned tokenization itself.

Several metrics have limitations that are not addressed: UTMOS exceeding ground truth raises calibration concerns; emotion consistency relies on an off-the-shelf classifier; duration consistency uses a very tight fixed tolerance; and no confidence intervals or statistical significance are reported.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper gives some training details, but omits many implementation specifics needed to reproduce results, such as data filtering, exact objective weights, optimizer schedules, tokenizer/vocoder preprocessing, alignment edge cases, and evaluation protocol details.

The novelty is meaningful but incremental relative to ASR-aligned representations, speech reconstruction tokenizers, supervised semantic tokens, and prior speech-text joint modeling. The paper would need stronger positioning and ablations to establish that TASTE is the key ingredient rather than an engineering combination of existing components.

Some claims are overstated, especially “extensive experiments,” “effective SLMs,” and “first end-to-end approach,” given the narrow downstream evaluation and limited discussion of closely related alignment/tokenization methods.
Presentation has recurring grammar issues, notation inconsistencies, and occasional unclear explanations, which do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence in the technical precision.

strengths: Uses a simple and computationally efficient layer-wise pruning criterion based on activation cosine similarity, making the method easy to implement and potentially practical for very large models.
Addresses an important problem: structured pruning of LLMs under tight calibration-data and compute budgets, with experiments spanning multiple model families and pruning ratios.
Includes several useful ablations, including the effect of calibration sample size, block size, similarity threshold, sparsity level, and comparisons to random and importance-based pruning variants.
Reports inference-time speedups and memory reductions, not only perplexity/accuracy, which is relevant for the claimed deployment motivation.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The central idea of using layer/block similarity or redundancy to remove transformer components is closely related to a substantial body of prior work on layer dropping, depth pruning, similarity-based pruning, and structured compression. The paper does not convincingly distinguish its contribution beyond a particular heuristic and thresholding recipe.

The empirical evidence is not strong enough for the breadth of the claims. Results are largely small-to-moderate improvements over selected baselines, and the paper does not establish robustness across stronger modern compression/distillation/pruning pipelines or post-pruning recovery methods.

The evaluation design leaves important gaps: downstream task results are limited, generation quality and instruction-following behavior are not deeply assessed, and there is little analysis of failure cases, domain shift, or sensitivity to calibration distribution despite the method relying directly on activation statistics.

Some comparisons appear potentially unfair or incomplete. Several baselines are not clearly tuned to comparable compute/data budgets, and the paper does not sufficiently separate gains from the proposed similarity criterion versus choices such as block grouping, layer reconstruction, or light fine-tuning.

Technical justification is weak. High cosine similarity between adjacent/block outputs is treated as evidence that layers can be removed, but the paper provides limited theoretical or mechanistic support that this preserves model function, especially when residual-stream interactions and later-layer amplification can make small differences matter.

Reproducibility is only partial. Key implementation details such as exact calibration prompts, threshold selection procedure, pruning schedules, fine-tuning hyperparameters, and baseline configurations need more precision for reliable reproduction.

The presentation overstates the significance of the method relative to the evidence. The paper frames the approach as broadly effective and generally applicable, but the experiments support a narrower conclusion: a simple heuristic can sometimes prune layers with tolerable degradation under the tested settings.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck in spoken language modeling: the severe length and representation mismatch between text tokens and speech tokens. The central idea of learning speech tokenization aligned to text token length is well motivated and likely useful for efficient joint speech-text modeling.

The proposed TASTE tokenizer is technically sensible: it leverages ASR initialization, cross-attention-based aggregation, RVQ discretization, and reconstruction training in a coherent architecture. The method is not merely an engineering tweak; it targets the tokenization stage where much of the modality gap originates.

The reconstruction results are promising. TASTE achieves competitive WER, speaker similarity, emotion consistency, and duration consistency at a much lower estimated bitrate than several speech tokenization baselines, suggesting that the representation preserves useful paralinguistic information despite aggressive compression.

The downstream SLM experiments are encouraging. TASLM performs competitively on SALMON acoustic evaluations and substantially improves over the S3-token baseline on StoryCloze, while using LoRA-based parameter-efficient adaptation from a 1B text LLM.

The paper is generally clear about the pipeline, model components, datasets, training phases, and evaluation metrics, and the method is presented in a way that should be understandable to readers familiar with speech language modeling.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is positive but not yet strong enough for a clear accept. Evaluation is limited to reconstruction on LibriTTS test-clean and likelihood-based SALMON/StoryCloze metrics. There is no human listening study, no subjective naturalness/similarity evaluation, and limited assessment of actual open-ended speech generation quality.

Important ablations are missing. The paper does not isolate the contributions of ASR initialization, the proposed shallow-value cross-attention aggregation, word-level averaging/alignment, RVQ depth/codebook size, frozen encoder choice, or token versus embedding modeling choices. This makes it hard to know which design decisions are essential.

Some comparisons are not fully convincing. Prior systems differ in model size, training data, training objective, and full fine-tuning versus LoRA, while the S3-token baseline appears quite weak and may not be optimally adapted. The paper would benefit from stronger controlled baselines using the same LLM, data, and tuning budget.

The method depends on text transcriptions or ASR outputs during tokenization and alignment. The paper assumes high-quality ASR and does not evaluate robustness to ASR errors, noisy speech, spontaneous speech, multilingual settings, or domain shift, all of which are central for practical spoken language modeling.

The reconstruction evaluation has confounds. TASTE is compared against methods with and without speaker embeddings, and the very high UTMOS score exceeding ground truth raises questions about whether the metric reflects true perceptual quality. More careful perceptual and statistical evaluation would strengthen the claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete. While many hyperparameters are reported, details on preprocessing, exact training data filtering, prompt/input formatting for SLM training, likelihood scoring, checkpoint release, code availability, and compute cost are insufficient for confident reproduction.

The paper does not substantially discuss risks or ethical issues related to speech generation, speaker similarity preservation, and possible voice misuse, despite proposing a tokenizer that retains speaker and emotion information.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: reducing the speech-text modality and length mismatch for joint spoken language modeling.

TASTE is conceptually simple and appealing: use text tokens as queries over frozen Whisper speech representations, quantize the resulting text-aligned speech embeddings, and then adapt a text LLM with aligned speech/text steps.

The work includes several relevant evaluation angles: reconstruction quality and similarity, text-aligned speech editing, speech continuation, likelihood-based SALMON/StoryCloze evaluation, and spoken QA.

The low-bitrate reconstruction results are promising: TASTE achieves competitive perceptual quality at about 150 bps and substantially improves over a text-only baseline while preserving some paralinguistic information.

The spoken language modeling results suggest practical value: TASLM improves strongly over the S3-token baseline and is competitive with or better than several prior SLMs on continuation and StoryCloze despite using a smaller base model.
weaknesses: The central evidence is not quite strong enough for a clear accept. Several comparisons are hard to interpret because methods differ in base LLM, training data, finetuning setup, vocoder, parameter count, and whether they are pretrained or instruction-tuned.

The method relies heavily on ASR transcripts and Whisper representations, but robustness to ASR errors, noisy transcripts, disfluencies, multilingual speech, and non-read speech is not evaluated. This is important because the tokenization is explicitly text-conditioned.

Ablations are insufficient for the main technical claims. The paper does not convincingly isolate the effects of text-aligned querying, last-layer keys versus shallow-layer values, RVQ configuration, word-level averaging, embedding versus token modeling, speaker embeddings, or reconstruction objective choices.

Some evaluation choices are weak. GPT-4o-based MOS over ASR transcripts is an indirect semantic metric; human continuation evaluation uses only 20 samples per method; and objective MOS metrics sometimes rate reconstructions above ground truth, raising concerns about overinterpreting these scores.

The reconstruction comparison is not fully apples-to-apples: TASTE uses text input and external speaker/vocoder machinery, while many codec/tokenizer baselines operate speech-only. The claimed bitrate advantage should be contextualized with this extra conditioning.

The acoustic benchmark results are mixed: TASLM improves over the S3 baseline but does not consistently outperform prior work on SALMON submetrics, and the paper’s aggregate presentation partly hides these weaknesses.

The spoken QA results are modest and comparisons are confounded by few-shot prompting versus instruction tuning and different base models; they support preservation of text-LM ability more than strong spoken understanding.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the abstract and conclusion mention demo/code/model availability, but the link appears blank, and many implementation details needed to reproduce data processing and evaluation are underspecified.

The paper makes fairly strong novelty and effectiveness claims, but related text-conditioned TTS/style-transfer and speech-text alignment work is only lightly discussed, leaving the exact novelty boundary somewhat underdeveloped.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: joint speech-text spoken language modeling is difficult partly because speech token streams are much longer than text token streams, and a text-aligned speech representation is a plausible way to simplify modeling.
weaknesses: The central efficiency and bitrate claims are not convincingly supported. The reconstruction decoder is conditioned on the text transcript as well as the TASTE tokens, yet the reported bitrate appears to count only the speech tokens. This makes comparisons against codecs such as EnCodec, Mimi, and SpeechTokenizer potentially unfair, since those methods reconstruct from audio tokens alone rather than from audio tokens plus textual side information.

The method is less end-to-end and less generally usable than the framing suggests. TASTE requires ASR transcripts to construct tokens, and the paper assumes sufficiently high-quality ASR. This is a strong dependency that may break under accented, noisy, multilingual, conversational, or domain-shifted speech, but these cases are not evaluated.

Novelty is moderate at best. The core mechanism is cross-attention from text tokens to frozen Whisper speech features followed by RVQ and reconstruction, combined with fairly standard LoRA-based SLM adaptation. The paper does not clearly separate what is genuinely new from a combination of existing ASR encoders, speech units, codec-style quantization, and text-speech attention.

The evaluation is not sufficiently controlled. The reconstruction experiments compare TASTE against tokenizers/codecs under different conditioning assumptions, and the spoken language modeling comparisons involve different base LMs, parameter counts, training data, and fine-tuning setups. This makes it hard to attribute gains specifically to text-aligned tokenization.

The human evaluation is too small for the strength of the claims: only 20 samples per method are used, with large standard deviations. Several claimed improvements, including comparisons to cascade systems, may not be statistically meaningful.

The speech continuation evaluation relies heavily on weak proxies. GPT-4o scores are computed from ASR transcriptions of generated speech, which conflates generation quality, ASR errors, and semantic coherence. UTMOS and DNSMOS are also proxy metrics and can be poorly calibrated for generated speech.

The method’s dependence on transcripts raises an important conceptual limitation: it may discard or underrepresent non-lexical speech phenomena, disfluencies, laughter, hesitations, overlapped speech, and paralinguistic events that are not faithfully represented in text. The paper claims preservation of paralinguistic information, but evaluates this only narrowly.

The ablation and analysis are insufficient. The paper lacks strong studies isolating the impact of the text-aligned attention design, the choice of Whisper layers, the use of S3/CosyVoice units, RVQ depth, transcript quality, word-level averaging, and the text-conditioning information leak in reconstruction.

The spoken QA results are weak evidence for broad understanding. TASLM slightly improves over its 1B text base under few-shot evaluation, but remains far behind stronger text and speech-text models; the comparison to instruction-tuned systems is not especially informative.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper says demo, code, and model are available, but the provided manuscript text does not include an actual link. Important details about training data filtering, evaluation prompts, decoding settings, significance tests, and exact bitrate computation are missing or under-specified.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful idea: learning speech tokens/embeddings that are explicitly aligned to text token positions, directly targeting a real obstacle in joint speech-text language modeling.

The method is technically plausible and relatively elegant, using frozen Whisper representations, cross-attention aggregation, RVQ, and reconstruction training to obtain compact text-aligned speech representations.
The experimental evidence is broad: reconstruction quality, bitrate, speech editing, continuation, likelihood-based SALMON/StoryCloze evaluation, and spoken QA are all considered.
The low-bitrate reconstruction results are compelling: TASTE achieves competitive perceptual quality and speaker similarity at roughly 150 bps, much lower than most compared tokenizers.
The spoken language modeling results are promising, especially the strong human MOS and StoryCloze performance with a 1.3B base model and LoRA adaptation.
The paper is generally well motivated and readable, with limitations acknowledged around latency, multilinguality, and lack of instruction-following dialogue behavior.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not fully controlled: competing SLMs differ in base LMs, training data, model size, tokenizers, and adaptation procedures, making it hard to isolate the benefit of TASTE itself.

Ablations are limited. The paper would be stronger with systematic studies of the aggregator design, use of last vs shallow Whisper layers, RVQ depth/codebook size, word-level averaging, reconstruction objective, and token vs embedding modeling choices.

The method depends on high-quality ASR transcripts during tokenization and modeling, but robustness to ASR errors, punctuation/tokenization errors, noisy speech, and out-of-domain speech is not evaluated.
The human evaluations are quite small: only 20 samples per method with about 10 ratings each, and the reported standard deviations are large for key continuation results.

Some evaluation choices are potentially fragile, especially GPT-4o-based semantic MOS over ASR transcripts and neural MOS predictors that can overestimate synthetic speech quality; stronger human and task-based validation would help.

The reconstruction tradeoff is mixed: TASTE has worse WER, ViSQOL, and duration consistency than several higher-bitrate baselines, so the claim of preserving paralinguistic information should be stated more carefully.

The spoken QA section is suggestive but not decisive because TASLM is compared against instruction-tuned systems and text baselines under different conditions; the few-shot setup is not described in enough detail.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the abstract and introduction mention demo/code/model availability, but the actual link appears missing, and many implementation details needed for replication are only lightly specified.

strengths: Clear and timely problem formulation: the paper targets the length and modality mismatch in joint text-speech spoken language modeling, and the proposed text-aligned speech tokenization is a natural and useful abstraction for hybrid decoding.

The method is technically coherent. Using text-token queries to aggregate Whisper speech representations, followed by RVQ and a reconstruction objective, gives a concrete way to produce speech tokens aligned one-to-one with text tokens without explicit forced alignment.

The empirical section is broader than typical for this area: reconstruction quality, continuation generation, likelihood-based SALMON/StoryCloze evaluation, spoken QA, editing demonstrations, module ablations, robustness to noise, and standard deviations are all reported.

Results support the main qualitative claim that very low-rate text-aligned speech tokens can preserve paralinguistic information beyond text-only reconstruction, especially in duration/speaker similarity and human MUSHRA.
The paper is generally well organized and includes useful implementation details, hyperparameters, human-evaluation instructions, limitations, and an ethics discussion around voice misuse.
weaknesses: The comparison to codec/tokenizer baselines is not fully apples-to-apples. TASTE is conditioned on text transcripts and speaker embeddings, while the reported bitrate appears to count only the speech token stream and not the text side information or speaker conditioning. This makes the dramatic bitrate advantage somewhat overstated.

The central SLM comparison is only partially controlled. TASLM is compared against prior pretrained SLMs with different base LMs, training data, objectives, decoding schemes, and parameter counts. The S3-token baseline helps, but stronger controlled baselines using the same LLaMA3.2-1B setup with alternative alignment/interleaving strategies would make the claim much more convincing.

The likelihood results are mixed: TASLM improves StoryCloze strongly but is clearly weaker than Spirit LM Expressive on SALMON overall, especially background/room attributes. The paper’s high-level claims about outperforming other SLMs need more nuance.

Continuation evaluation relies partly on GPT-4o scoring ASR transcripts and a small human test of 20 samples per method. This is useful but not enough to fully establish open-ended generation quality, robustness, or semantic coherence across domains.

The method inherits important limitations from ASR-based tokenization: it assumes good transcripts, is evaluated only in English, and is less suited for non-lexical vocalizations, overlapping speech, environmental sounds, or speech without reliable word segmentation. These are acknowledged but still materially narrow the scope.

Novelty is meaningful but incremental relative to existing text-conditioned speech reconstruction, TTS style/prosody control, and joint speech-text modeling. The main contribution is a clean integration and demonstration for SLMs rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as rendered: the abstract says demo/code/models are available but no visible URL is provided. Several components also depend on pretrained external systems and large-scale Emilia training, which may make exact reproduction difficult.

strengths: The paper identifies a real pain point in joint text-speech modeling: conventional speech token streams are much longer than text streams and require nontrivial alignment/interleaving heuristics.

The proposed TASTE representation is simple and potentially useful: text-conditioned attention aggregates speech encoder states into a sequence aligned to transcript tokens, enabling straightforward joint modeling.

The paper reports a fairly broad set of experiments, including reconstruction metrics, speech continuation, likelihood-based benchmarks, spoken QA, module ablations, ASR-vs-ground-truth ablations, and robustness to noise.
The very low token rate/bitrate is an interesting practical property, and the text-aligned editing examples suggest the representation may capture word-local paralinguistic information.
weaknesses: The central comparison to speech tokenizers/codecs is not fully fair: TASTE receives text/transcripts as an explicit side channel, so its low bitrate and reconstruction quality are not directly comparable to speech-only codecs unless the text channel cost and ASR dependence are accounted for.

The novelty is moderate. The method combines a frozen ASR encoder, cross-attention aggregation, RVQ, and an existing S3/vocoder target pipeline. The paper overstates the contribution as an end-to-end tokenizer while relying heavily on pretrained Whisper, S3 units, a pretrained vocoder, and LLM LoRA adaptation.

The main SLM evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier venue. Baselines differ in base models, model sizes, training recipes, tokenizers, and likely data exposure; the weak S3-token baseline may not represent a strong implementation of non-text-aligned joint modeling.

Several reported gains could be driven mostly by the text transcript/LLM path rather than by the proposed speech tokens. In particular, StoryCloze and QA results may primarily measure preservation of text-LM ability, while SALMON performance is mixed and weak for background/acoustic conditions.

Human evaluation is small and fragile: only 20 samples per method are used, standard deviations are large, and there is no clear statistical significance analysis. GPT-4o-based MOS via ASR transcription is also an indirect and potentially biased semantic metric.

The paper evaluates mostly English, single-speaker-style/read speech settings and does not demonstrate robustness for multilingual speech, overlapping speakers, non-lexical events, dialogue, turn-taking, streaming, or realistic noisy interactive use cases, despite positioning the work as a spoken language modeling advance.

Some technical details are underspecified or questionable, including the exact text query embeddings used in the aggregator, how ASR tokenization and LLM tokenization are reconciled in practice, and whether word-level averaging/replication undermines the clean one-to-one alignment claim.

The ethical discussion acknowledges voice manipulation risks but offers no concrete safeguards, misuse evaluation, watermarking/provenance mechanism, or deployment constraints, which is concerning given that text-aligned speech editing is presented as a capability.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and timely contribution: text-aligned speech tokenization/embedding that directly targets the length and modality mismatch in joint text-speech spoken language modeling.

The technical idea is simple but effective: cross-attention from text tokens to speech encoder states produces one speech representation per text token, enabling straightforward simultaneous text and speech token modeling.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this area, covering reconstruction quality, perceptual similarity, speech continuation, likelihood-based benchmarks, spoken QA, editing behavior, ASR sensitivity, robustness to noise, and several ablations.

Results are compelling: TASTE achieves competitive reconstruction at extremely low bitrate, and TASLM substantially improves over prior pretrained SLMs on continuation quality while remaining competitive on likelihood-based semantic/acoustic evaluations.
The paper includes useful diagnostic evidence, including module ablations, shallow-layer analysis, cross-attention visualizations, ASR-vs-ground-truth comparisons, and standard deviations.
The work is well positioned relative to recent SLM and codec/tokenizer literature, and the limitations and misuse risks of voice synthesis/editing are explicitly discussed.
weaknesses: The method depends on ASR-derived text, so it is less general than textless SLMs and may struggle in domains where ASR is unreliable, such as noisy, multilingual, code-switched, overlapping, or non-lexical speech. The ASR ablations are useful but mostly within favorable English settings.

The strongest results are on English read or relatively clean speech, especially LibriSpeech/LibriTTS-style evaluation; multilingual, conversational, real-time, multi-speaker, and non-speech audio generalization remain largely untested.

Some comparisons are not perfectly controlled: prior SLMs differ in base model, training data, decoding setup, and adaptation strategy, while the S3-token baseline is helpful but may not cover all strong alternatives for fair joint modeling.
The human evaluation is relatively small, with 20 samples per method, so the perceptual conclusions are encouraging but not definitive, especially given the large standard deviations.
The paper reports that code/models/demo are available, but the manuscript text appears to omit the actual URL, which weakens reproducibility as submitted.

TASTE performs poorly on SALMON background/room attributes, indicating that the representation discards or fails to model some acoustic context that may matter for broader spoken-language understanding.
The safety discussion identifies voice imitation and speech editing misuse, but concrete safeguards, watermarking, consent enforcement, or abuse evaluation are not part of the technical contribution.
